header: Date: 2028-07-21 | Time: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 56m | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Marco (Polaris Head of Platform), Aisha (Infra), Sam (ML), Lena (Security)
summary: Customer reported intermittent p99 spikes when routing requests through VPC on-prem gateway. Main questions: impact of streaming vs non-streaming (batching) on tail, KV cache shard hotness across multi-path networks, and quantized model cold-start behavior on onprem GPUs. Redwood SE to run targeted bench and share traces; next meeting to review results and discuss fallback/topology changes.
topics: on-prem GPU topology and autoscaling impact
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll do a quick run through agenda then dive into the tail traces you sent, um, does that work for folks?
[00:06] Marco Rinaldi: yeah that works, thanks Jordan. We really want to get to the p99 spikes, they're killing real time features.
[00:12] Priya Desai: cool, quick intros? I'll be the SE, Priya, focused on runtime and perf. Ethan's on the call for kernel/quant questions.
[00:18] Aisha Khan: hi I'm Aisha, infra lead, mainly network/VPC and on-prem setup.
[00:22] Sam Cho: Sam, ML engineer, I'm the owner of the model and request patterns.
[00:25] Lena Ortiz: Lena, security, will ask about audit/KMS stuff as we go.
[00:28] Jordan Kim: perfect. Ok first, Marco shared three traces — one for hosted routing through our dedicated pool, one for VPC egress through Polaris on-prem gateway with multi-path, and one for pure on-prem deployment. We'll screen share the first trace.
[00:42] Priya Desai: uh quick note, transcription might flip some words in the trace, e.g., KV cache sometimes transcribed as K-V cash which is weird.
[00:49] Marco Rinaldi: yeah sorry about that. So our symptom: p95 is fine at ~120ms but p99 jumps to ~950-1.2s intermittently, mostly during midday traffic surges. We see this only when requests traverse our VPC edge proxy to the on-prem cluster, not when calling hosted.
[01:05] Priya Desai: ok that already suggests a network multipath amplification — packets taking a longer route or a stalled connection to a particular KV shard. Did you correlate to KV hit/miss?
[01:14] Sam Cho: we saw a slight uptick in KV miss rate during spikes, but not huge, like 3->7 percent. We do have sharding by user region, but some shards are hotter.
[01:23] Ethan Brooks: can you confirm shard mapping? Hot shards often correlate with tail when you have a congested NIC or faulty route.
[01:31] Aisha Khan: yes our sharding is basic modulo by org id, we haven't localized hot shards to physical hosts, that's on the list. Also we use a haproxy front to route to backends, and there are two network paths to the compute racks — sometimes traffic picks the longer path via the storage VLAN.
[01:45] Priya Desai: did you capture tcp_retransmits or RST spikes? Because retransmits add latency and we see them show up in 99th.
[01:51] Marco Rinaldi: we did capture some retransmits, around the same window.
[01:55] Jordan Kim: ok so hypothesis A: network multipath + retransmit causing occasional 800-1,200ms tails. Hypothesis B: KV cache hot-shard cold miss plus on-prem model cold-start on quantized kernels. We should test both.
[02:10] Sam Cho: on model cold-start — we run quantized 4-bit weights on NVIDIA A10s with Triton; cold starts can add ~200-300ms for kernel JIT on first tokens.
[02:20] Ethan Brooks: when you say JIT do you mean CUDA kernel warm-up or our runtime's cuJIT fallback? Sometimes Triton or CuBLASJK creates new contexts that cost time.
[02:29] Sam Cho: yes, exactly, we see kernels compiling on first call if we don't pin the process or keep a keepalive.
[02:35] Priya Desai: streaming vs non-streaming aspect — with streaming we keep the KV cache open and reuse KV cache across requests, but streaming also increases exposed hop count because we maintain a longer-lived connection, potentially more vulnerable to path flaps. In batch (non-streaming) we pay per-request overhead but we can combine prefix caching and reduce per-token overhead via batching.
[02:55] Jordan Kim: quick interjection: can someone share the typical prompt length and token distribution? It drives batching benefits.
[03:02] Sam Cho: 95% of requests are short prompts, 12–40 tokens generation, tail cases include long dialogs at ~300 tokens but rare.
[03:10] Priya Desai: that profile means batching can help throughput but may not reduce p99 for short-latency use cases — batching can increase average throughput but if one request in a batch hits a slow shard you'll amplify p99.
[03:23] Marco Rinaldi: so does that mean streaming is safer for p99? We thought streaming would reduce p99 because partial results are returned earlier.
[03:31] Priya Desai: streaming can reduce perceived latency for first bytes but doesn't eliminate backend stalls — if the request stalls while waiting on a hot KV or a retransmit, streaming will still show a pause in the stream. The p99 of final token can still be high. Also we need to check whether you use prefix caching; streaming with prefix cached reduces work.
[03:50] Aisha Khan: hmm, ok. On the network side, we have two egress paths; one goes through our colo provider east, another goes via a path that crosses an extra hop through their backbone. We suspect BGP flaps occasionally reroute.
[04:02] Jordan Kim: do you have traceroutes that line up with the p99 windows?
[04:06] Aisha Khan: we do some periodic traceroutes but not correlated with timestamps, we can run targeted probes.
[04:11] Priya Desai: action: instrument traceroute and tcpdump at the times we re-run the bench. Priya to provide a bench harness config.
[04:18] Sam Cho: question on quantization: when you switch models to an 8-bit or 4-bit kernel, do you recommend keeping a warm pool of workers?
[04:26] Ethan Brooks: yes. For quantized kernels we recommend a pinned worker pool with warm memory residency. That avoids per-request initialization and reduces cold-start tail. In Redwood you can set a min-pool size on Dedicated/Private.
[04:37] Marco Rinaldi: we run in Private on our k8s cluster, we use nodeAffinity to pin to GPU nodes but we didn't set a warm pool. Is there a recommended memory/cpu for warm pool?
[04:47] Priya Desai: for A10s and short prompts, a 2-worker pinned pool per shard is a good start. Monitor OOMs. Also ensure you pre-load KV shard metadata into the runtime process to reduce miss penalty.
[04:59] Jordan Kim: can we talk about KV cache architecture — you mentioned modulo sharding. That can cause cross-host hotness. If your routing isn't shard-aware (nearby routing), it can route a user to a node that doesn't hold the shard and then do an inter-node call, adding network latency.
[05:13] Sam Cho: oh yeah our haproxy does simple round robin to a pod set; it doesn't use shard locality.
[05:18] Priya Desai: that matches the symptom — a request for a hot key lands on a pod that proxies to the shard owner causing an extra hop. That extra hop can be in the 100–300ms range if saturated or retransmitting, explaining p99 spikes.
[05:29] Lena Ortiz: for security, if we change routing to shard-aware, does that require additional ACLs? We have strict East-West policies.
[05:36] Aisha Khan: we already have overlay network policies, but yes we'd need to make sure pod-to-pod access is allowed; should be doable.
[05:41] Priya Desai: recommended changes: 1) make routing shard-aware (haproxy x-header or use local-lb per shard), 2) pin warm workers per shard to avoid cold quant kernel starts, 3) add traceroute/tcpdump on suspect windows, 4) consider streaming for user perceived latency but still pursue shard-awareness to lower backend p99.
[05:58] Marco Rinaldi: sounds good. Can you quantify the expected p99 improvement?
[06:02] Priya Desai: rough order: removing the extra inter-node hop can drop the 99th by 200–500ms in your environment, pinning warm workers another 100–250ms for cold-starts, and reducing retransmits via path fixes another 100–300ms; combined you can see p99 drop from ~1.2s to sub-400–500ms in many cases. But must validate.
[06:21] Sam Cho: ok we'll try shard-aware routing. One practical concern: rebalancing during autoscaling causing shard ownership changes. Does Redwood have recommendations?
[06:30] Ethan Brooks: yes, ideally use consistent hashing with virtual nodes so remaps are minimal; and coordinate rebalancing during low-traffic windows. Our runtime supports sticky routing tokens so you can reassign shards gradually.
[06:41] Aisha Khan: latency of the consistent hash lookups? negligible?
[06:44] Priya Desai: negligible compared to network hops — it's a local lookup.
[06:48] Jordan Kim: let's discuss tests we'll run. Priya, can you outline the microbench?
[06:52] Priya Desai: sure. Bench plan: three configs (hosted via Redwood, VPC egress via Polaris gateway, on-prem private). For each: 1) baseline single-stream no batching, 2) streaming keepalive, 3) batching with 5-10ms aggregation windows and max batch 8, 4) warm-pool enabled vs cold. We'll capture tcpdump, traceroute, and runtime traces (span ids) and produce p50/p95/p99 and token-level latencies.
[07:18] Marco Rinaldi: timeframe?
[07:20] Priya Desai: I'll run host+VPC tests in our infra and then coordinate with Polaris for on-prem; expect results in 6 days. Jordan will share the bench harness and config now.
[07:29] Jordan Kim: I'll post the harness link and the minimal config to your slack channel and DM. For security docs, Lena, we have SOC2 excerpt and KMS integration guide. I'll attach them.
[07:39] Lena Ortiz: appreciate that. Also do you capture audit logs for each request in Private? We need proof of per-token provenance.
[07:45] Priya Desai: we emit request-level audit logs with model version, route, and token counts — we can increase retention for the pilot.
[07:51] Sam Cho: on retransmits — if we see TCP retransmits aligned with p99 windows, do you recommend fixing BGP or using a second static path?
[07:59] Aisha Khan: we can set up a static tunnel as fallback during pilot.
[08:03] Priya Desai: good. Also consider small MTU misconfig or SMB offload causing retransmits — capture MSS/flags on tcpdump.
[08:12] Jordan Kim: any questions about model quantization impacts?
[08:15] Sam Cho: curious if Redwood runtime adds any additional quant conversion at runtime; we pre-quantize models to 4-bit but still have to wrap tensors in runtime.
[08:23] Ethan Brooks: our runtime supports direct tensor layout for quantized weights — no runtime conversion if saved in supported layout. Edge cases exist with certain operator fusions where we fallback to a generic kernel and that adds latency. We'll check your model's op pattern.
[08:37] Priya Desai: please upload a sample model op list (torchscript or model.json) and we'll run a quick compatibility check.
[08:44] Sam Cho: will do.
[08:46] Marco Rinaldi: will you need direct access to our on-prem cluster for the bench?
[08:50] Jordan Kim: ideally yes, for the on-prem run. We can use a short-lived bastion or run bench agents you deploy. We'll provide IaC snippets.
[08:58] Aisha Khan: we prefer bench agents rather than opening SSH.
[09:01] Jordan Kim: that's fine. We'll send a dockerized bench agent.
[09:04] Priya Desai: one more note about streaming: if you care about first-byte latency only, streaming can mask backend tail by emitting partial tokens early, but the end-to-end p99 for conversation closure still depends on backend stalls. Workload matters.
[09:18] Marco Rinaldi: ok makes sense. Any objections to starting with shard-aware routing + warm pool as the first changes?
[09:24] Aisha Khan: no objections. We'll provision network rules.
[09:27] Lena Ortiz: security sign-off required but not a blocker.
[09:30] Jordan Kim: great. Let's recap actions — Priya runs bench and shares traces; Jordan shares bench harness and security pack; Sam provides model op list and request profile; Marco/Aisha to run network probes and allow bench agents. We'll meet next week to review.
[09:46] Priya Desai: thanks all. I'll tack on a small doc describing how to interpret the p99 traces and the span ids we emit, that way you can map network hops to runtime spans.
[09:56] Jordan Kim: thanks everyone. Meeting end.
